articles.text: There is no more admired person in human history than Jesus of Nazareth. His name is often invoked. Millions worship him regularly. His followers pray as he taught them to pray and are known to offer loving service, as well as go to war, in his name. Yet, fierce debates rage as to exact nature of his being, the true essence of his ministry, the most accurate definition of his theology. I would be remiss to suggest that my sermon this morning will resolve these. They are likely to continue for centuries to come. I would humbly suggest that regardless of our faith backgrounds, religious traditions or our theological positions, we can find unity in the simple affirmation that Jesus is inspiring. One of the earliest hymns about Jesus is quoted by Paul in chapter 2 of his letter to the followers of Jesus in Philippi, a major commercial center of the Roman Empire located in northern Greece. In this warm letter Paul quotes two verses of what scholars call the Kenotic Hymn, the Greek work kenosis (empty) being central to the theology he wants to lift up. Paul writes, “Let the same mind be in you that was in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be exploited, but emptied himself” I hear him saying. articles.text: The City of Piedmont sent out an online survey on September 28 to community members asking for input on housing plans for Moraga Canyon. This marks the beginning of public engagement with the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan – an initiative that will study all City-owned land in Moraga Canyon with the goal of creating detailed housing plans for possible development in the future. “It’s a good opportunity to have Piedmont community members respond and voice their concerns and responses,” said Kevin Jackson, the city’s Planning Director. “We’re trying to move this project forward and engage with the community. It’ll be a stronger plan with greater community engagement.” These efforts are part of a larger initiative by the City of Piedmont to add housing units to the community. A recent mandate by the state of California requires cities to plan additional housing units in their communities to help meet housing needs across the state. The City of Piedmont was charged with creating plans to accommodate 587 units of new housing, including 257 affordable units by 2031. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan proposes to build 132 units of new housing (60 of which would be for low-income households). SURVEY QUESTIONS Among other things, the survey asks what community members the following: • When you visit Moraga Canyon, how do you and/or your family spend your time there? • What concerns do you have about new housing development in Moraga Canyon? • Would you be interested in living in multifamily housing in Moraga Canyon? Other questions ask citizens to rank the buildings they would like to see in Moraga Canyon based on architectural style with a scale from 1 to 5. The survey is available at piedmont.ca.gov/MoragaCanyonSurvey and will remain open through October 20th. articles.text: You might see something new as you pass by the construction site for Piedmont’s new community pool being built. On Wednesday, September 27, construction workers sprayed concrete on the retaining walls. Concrete was added to the walls using “shotcrete,” a method of applying concrete to a surface with a high-pressure hose at high velocity. – George Sanen Construction Manager Piedmont Community Pool “You’re going to start seeing the outlines of buildings,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. He said that current work will help the community visualize the progress of construction. Staff photos Construction workers spray concrete onto the retaining walls at the community pool construction site. Members of various city departments were present for an on-site tour. On-site Construction Manager George Sanen led the group through the project site, stopping at several places to talk about the work being done. “This will be the second all-electric public swimming pool in the country,” Sanen told the group on the tour. “If everything Pool construction manager George Sanen leads a group of city officials through the project site. George Sanen speaks with Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works. goes well, by this time next year, we’ll be swimming.” Sanen also commented on the necessary maintenance that the pool will need after construction is complete. “I use the reference of buying a Ferrari. The city is buying a Ferrari and so the city needs different experts with experience to properly operate and maintain [the pool].” The community pool has experienced minor construction delays in recent weeks. In July, the discovery of an underground 100-year-old fuel tank created complications for the City. Because the tank still contained gasoline, it was considered a toxic substance, and the city was required to submit an inspection and work plan to the County of Alameda for its removal. Since then, the fuel has been pumped out of the tank and the surrounding soil has been successfully checked to confirm no contamination exists. The tank was removed from site on Friday, September 29. Gonzales also said that workers have also been digging holes for gas, water, and Comcast lines for future facilities at the pool site. “Most of our timeline depends upon when PG&E can install the power source.” PG&E has not yet provided a date to come to the site. Construction is currently scheduled to finish in September 2024. For more information on the Piedmont Community Pool project, visit piedmont.ca.gov/newpool. articles.text: The annual Piedmont Artisanal Beer Festival, which takes place this Friday at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, will feature the concoctions of around a dozen local home brewers. One of them is Brian Black, a dad of two recent Piedmont graduates and husband of Piedmont High School English teacher Beth Black. Black’s academic discipline as a molecular biologist turned into work as a cardiovascular scientist at UCSF. It also furnished him with a scientific lens for his hobby as a beermaker. On Friday evening he will bring two ales to share, Shelterwood Ale, an American Pale Ale, and Monastic Whisper, a Belgian Dubbel. Black’s pathway to brewing from the field of medicine and biology helped him start higher on the brewing learning curve. “Brewing is kind of a mix of microbiology, chemistry, and engineering,” Black explained. His professional passion also led him to install equipment in his Oakland home conducive to science and brewing. Two large ovens in his kitchen help him sterilize all brewing equipment. “Anyone can make good beer if they can follow a recipe if – and it’s a big if – if they can keep stuff sterile or sanitized,” he said. “If you can get your equipment sterile, your homebrew will at least be decent, if not outstanding.” It was when making a Kölsch, a type of ale from Cologne, Germany, that his passion for brewing sparked. “The first time I tried a more challenging style, what really solidified my desire to be a hobbyist was when I made a Kölsch. It’s a narrow style, with a narrow alcohol range, color range, bitterness range, and a very specific type of yeast that has to be used.” Living just outside of Piedmont, Black’s hillside yard allows him to grow two kinds of hops, enough to make at least one SMaSH (Single Malt and Single Hop) every year. “Beer [brewing] is basically wort, which is a sweet and bitter soup, and then we keep it sterile. We put the yeast that we want in there, they eat the sugar, and they produce carbon dioxide and alcohol – and that’s beer making,” Black explained. Black will be at the beer festival with a dozen other homebrewers this Friday at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue, from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. The beer festival includes a freshly prepared German dinner on the lawn in front of the Center. articles.text: This year’s goal is $3.5 million to minimize school funding gap Fall is here and school is back in the swing of things. The Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign launched on Tuesday, September 19, with a week of celebration. It included a large number of community members wearing purple and kids enjoying popsicles in the park donated by Mulberry’s Market. That evening PEF hosted a New Parent Party at the Community Center followed by a Lead Donor Party hosted at the beautiful home of Melissa and Ali Partovi. This year’s campaign chairs are Catie Osborn and Kim Hunter, supported by the PEF team and a group of dedicated volunteers. Over the next few months, the team will work to raise funds for Piedmont’s students, putting up banners at schools, conducting community outreach, writing personal letters and making phone calls. The campaign is a response to California’s chronic underfunding of public schools. This year, the team asks that families donate $2,132 per student to help make up the gap between what is needed and what the state provides to Piedmont schools. “A great education requires great teachers,” Heather Frank, PEF Executive Director, told the Board of Education on September 27. “While state and parcel tax funding make up the bulk of PUSD’s budget, the more we raise through the Giving Campaign, the stronger Piedmont schools will become.” Campaign co-chair Catie Osborn captured it perfectly in a speech during kick-off week: “The Giving Campaign is particularly important this year because it is critical that we continue to retain and attract the highest quality teachers and staff. Everyone knows, teachers and staff are our greatest asset. Almost 80% of the PEF grant goes towards teacher and staff salaries.” The funds from last year’s Giving Campaign is helping to fund small class sizes, wellness and college development programs, lunchtime libraries, the arts, and much more. It is an investment in the children and the community. Piedmont has always been known for its outstanding education system and the community’s investment is key. articles.text: Happy Halloween! Many kids (and adults) love celebrating Halloween traditions with costumes, decorations, trick-or-treating and displaying a jack-o’-lantern on the front steps. Celebrating these traditions not only creates lifelong memories, but also allows opportunities for supporting speech and language development. Here are some of my favorite ways to integrate speech and language skills into your holiday traditions. 1. Pumpkin Carving & Painting Pumpkin carving/painting is a fantastic way to promote speech and language development. Whether you pick out your pumpkin from a patch or the grocery store, there is an abundance of variety in your pumpkin options. This allows your child to practice using descriptive vocabulary in the selection process. For example, your child can practice describing size (little, small, tiny, medium, big, large, huge, tall, giant, gigantic, enormous), shape (circle, round, oval), color (orange, yellow, white, green), texture (smooth, bumpy, dented, curve, lines, crack), and weight (heavy, light). This is also a great opportunity to model the use of comparatives (this is big, but this one is bigger, and that one is the biggest). After selecting the perfect pumpkin, it’s time to carve or paint. To work on developing sequencing and narrative language, you can talk about the steps to carving a pumpkin before (or after) you carve your pumpkin. Narrate the following steps for your child: • First cut off the top • Second scoop out the seeds • Then draw the eyes, nose, mouth Halloween can be a learning opportunity for young kids. • Next cut out the eyes, nose, mouth • Last, put a candle or light inside For children who benefit from visual support, take pictures along the way. 2. “Trick-or-Treating” Trick or treating is for everyone. Halloween is an amazing time to practice communication during a super motivating activity (free candy), but remember Halloween is about fun and not about explaining why your child isn’t communicating verbally. This allows your child to practice using descriptive vocabulary in the selection process. For example, your child can practice describing size (little, small, tiny, medium, big, large, huge, tall, giant, gigantic, enormous), shape (circle, round, oval), color (orange, yellow, white, green), texture (smooth, bumpy, dented, curve, lines, crack), and weight (heavy, light). This is also a great opportunity to model the use of comparatives (this is big, but this one is bigger, and that one is the biggest). After selecting the perfect pumpkin, it’s time to carve or paint. To work on developing sequencing and narrative language, you can talk about the steps to carving a pumpkin before (or after) you carve your pumpkin. Narrate the following steps for your child: • First cut off the top • Second scoop out the seeds • Then draw the eyes, nose, mouth Halloween can be a learning opportunity for young kids. • Next cut out the eyes, nose, mouth • Last, put a candle or light inside For children who benefit from visual support, take pictures along the way. 2. “Trick-or-Treating” Trick or treating is for everyone. Halloween is an amazing time to practice communication during a super motivating activity (free candy), but remember Halloween is about fun and not about explaining why your child isn’t communicating verbally. For children who have difficulty with communicating, trick-ortreating can be a difficult task and we must find different ways to include all children that would like to participate. To capitalize on this, you can provide simple cards, or use pre-programmed recordings that say things along the lines of trick or treat, happy halloween and/or thank you to allow children to have fun, be successful communicators, and have A LOT of practice communicating and receiving a fun reward. 3. Candy Sorting After trick-or-treating, have your child sort the candy by color, size, shape or candy type (chocolate/gummy, hard/soft). This activity is a great way to work on descriptive vocabulary, comparing/contrasting, categorization, and quantitative concepts (e.g., you have more M&Ms than skittles). 4 Playing “Guess the costume” Children love playing guessing games. Students had choices of 10 activities related to the history of Medieval times, such as stilt walking and sword fighting. Favorite activities also included Medieval Hopscotch and games of cornhole using bean bags. articles.text: At the lovely Medieval Banquet before students went outside to take part in the different activities, everyone sat in the Multi-Purpose Room to enjoy a feast of juice and cookies. They did this while watching the different forms of entertainment that the core classes created. Before going to the MPR, people from all grades watched the Maypole dance on the main patio in front of the school. Ms. Brenemann’s class showed everyone their hard work. All the students in her class either held the pole, tossed flowers around, or weaved all the ribbons into an intricate design. The next entertainment was when the king and queen were presented. Two rows of students from Ms. Keenan’s class stood parallel to a red paper carpet as music played. The kids on the sides danced while the king and queen walked down the “carpet.” The king and queen then took their place and sat down wearing their thrones. Before everyone could eat, Mr. Scherman’s class presented a skit called “Don’t Put Your Whole Hand in the Pot.” It showed the seven rules about eating in Medieval times using seven groups and eight narrators. The rules included: clean your nails before eating, don’t pick your nose and then eat, and don’t pick or clean your teeth with a knife. Some other rules were: don’t be the first to reach into the pot, use a napkin or the tablecloth to wipe your hands, don’t put your used bones back in the pot, and take the first piece of food that you touch. The second of the three dances was the circle dance performed by another one of Ms. Brenemann’s classes. The students all started in rows, then formed into groups of four and danced in a circle formation. As the dance went on, this class formed circles of many different sizes and danced in many different ways. The final form of entertainment was the Stick Dance performed by Ms. Kelly’s core class. It was very well practiced and was interesting. The students started in two rows and banged silver sticks on the ground like drums. They rose and fell in unison, and the sounds as well as the visual represented how amazing the dance was. The dance also included scenes of sword fighting with each person changing partners several times.

articles.text: Photos by Rob Peterson Piedmont players celebrate after defeating Bishop O’Dowd for the first time in 30 years. Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team accomplished something they haven’t achieved in nearly three decades. On Tuesday, September 26, they beat Bishop O’Dowd 3-2 in a five-set donnybrook played before a home court crowd at Binks Rawlings Gym. articles.text: Now in October, each team is identifying leaders to help propel their programs towards playoffs. Here we take a look at four key athletes this fall: Sam Shelby, football; Sadie Town, volleyball; George Stein, water polo; and Dahlia Osman, flag football. Sam Shelby, Football Sam Shelby, a junior, is putting together quite the season on the gridiron, showing his speed as a track sprinter and soccer winger. He’s totaled 20 receptions for 400 yards and five touchdowns, to go along with nine rushing attempts for 137 yards and two touchdowns. He dominated in Piedmont’s 41-3 win over Encinal on September 15 with five receptions for 139 yards and two touchdowns. He also put up seven catches for 154 yards and two touchdowns in their 46-7 win over Mt. Eden. In the season-opening 33-21 loss to Pierce on August 25, he had with seven receptions for 102 yards and a touchdown. Shelby is set to play against Alameda on Saturday, October 7 after incorrectly being suspended against Arroyo. PHS successfully appealed the ruling with video evidence of no “violent conduct” by Shelby. Sadie Town, Volleyball Sadie Town, a senior, was identified as a leader at the end of last season as the school’s leading outside hitter. She’s taken on the same role this fall, helping lead Piedmont to a 7-9 record thus far, with improvement shown each week. Her recent 28-kill performance against Bishop O’Dowd led Piedmont to one of its only wins over the Dragons in school history. Her achievement was the highest number of spikes in a single game since Samantha Fanger recorded 24 in 2017. It goes down as one of the best offensive performances in team history. Town also had 18 kills against Berkeley, 14 against Head-Royce, and 13 against San Leandro. George Stein, Water Polo George Stein, another senior, is a leader on the water polo team and a three-year starter. He’s emerged as a leading scorer on this year’s team after putting in five goals in a recent 13-9 win over Newark on September 27. He also scored four goals in a 10-9 win over Newark at the Labor Day Bash on September 2. He scored a 3-goal hat trick in a 14-6 loss to Terra Linda and four goals in a 10-2 win over Mission San Jose at the Labor Day Bash. Although the “Falls” is more of a trickle given that it is active only after a heavy rain, the walk shows you what makes Mt. Tam so magnificent. At times, you will pass through narrow corridors of redwood trees that appear to be out of a fairytale. Starting at the Dawn Falls Trailhead on Madrone Avenue in Larkspur, the trail along the inactive Larkspur Creek is a palette of vibrant fall colors from maple leaves; redwoods tower over in every direction, while lush green moss covers every tree, stone, and branch. It is worth mentioning that the Dawn Falls Trail is a mostly a slim passage, generally less than three feet wide. Patience is required when passing by hikers, runners, and large groups on weekends. Our 10 a.m. walk up to the falls passed a staggering 49 people in the 1.5 miles, passing another 34 people in the remaining two miles back to the car – making 83 people passed in total, so near 24 other patrons per mile. For those conscious of personal space, continue on the Southern Marin Line Fire Road; a dirt road which is wide enough to adequate two lanes of cars. Otherwise, you can continue up the Hoo Koo E Koo Trail and Blithedale Ridge trails, which will more than double your elevation gain to provide a workout of near 1,200 feet until re-intersecting with the fire road. You’ll get glimpses of Mt. Tam’s eastern peak from the fire road, a location we last visited over the summer. The 0.5 mile walk down the Barbara Springs Trail back to the car is a very steep 500- foot descent back with tree roots shooting out in every direction – so be wary. You’ll likely have to use your hands at various points. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on November 25, 2020. articles.text: Tickets available for Dance Series One October 5 - 7 Smuin Ballet’s Dance Series One will be performed in San Francisco on October 7. San Francisco-based dance company Smuin Ballet will close its Dance Series One at the Cowell Theater in San Francisco’s Fort Mason this Saturday, October 7. Tickets are still available for performances Thursday through Saturday. The program includes The Man in Black by James Kudelka, Tutto Eccetto il Lavandino (Everything but the Kitchen Sink) by Val Caniparoli, and the world premiere of Salsa ’til Dawn by Darrell Grand Moultrie. The performance opens with longtime Smuin collaborator Caniparoli’s Tutto Eccetto il Lavandino. It is a playful, energetic piece that premiered in 2014 and has been an audience favorite since. Kudelka’s The Man in Black is a ballad-style piece with choreography set to songs recorded by Johnny Cash, a country singer-songwriter whose music often contained themes of sorrow, moral tribulation and redemption. The dance celebrates working-class grit, and includes American country dance styles like line dancing, square, swing and step. The ballet premiered in 2010. The upcoming performance also features the world premiere of Moultrie’s Salsa ’til Dawn, with music by Charles Fox. Composer Fox collaborated with company founder Michael Smuin on two ballets, A Song for Dead Warriors, commissioned for the San Francisco Ballet, and Zorro!. His entire output of music is soon to be recognized at the Library of Congress. “Music is always the complete inspiration for me,” said Moultrie. “It’s been such an honor to work with an artistic giant like Charles [Fox} and bring his music to life by marrying it with the physicality of dance.” Visit https://www.smuinballet. org/events/dance-series-one-30/ to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s POTUS: Or, Behind Every Great Dumbass are Seven Women Trying to Keep Him Alive is being performed on stage now through October 22. The comedic take on White House events is a feminist-focused satire, premiering in time for presidential primaries. When the president unknowingly spins a public relations nightmare into a global crisis, seven brilliant but beleaguered women must risk it all to keep the commander-in-chief out of trouble. The play features Harriet Deirdre Lovejoy as chief of staff, Kim Blanck as press secretary, Susan Lynskey as secretary, Stephanie Pope Lofgren as the first lady, Dominique Toney as a journalist, Stephanie Styles as the president’s dalliance and Allison Guinn as his sister. POTUS is written by Selina Fillinger and directed by Annie Tippe. Post-show discussions are held tomorrow, October 5, and on October 10, guided by members of Berkeley Rep’s artistic team. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/potus/. articles.text: Michael Tilson Thomas, the longtime Music Director of San Francisco Symphony, returns from retirement to lead the symphony in performances of Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9 on Thursday, October 19, and Saturday and Sunday, October 21 and 22. The program includes Olly Wilson’s Shango Memory. Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9 in D minor, Op. 125, is a choral symphony, completed between 1822 and 1824 and first performed in Vienna on May 7, 1824. Many critics and musicologists regard it as a masterpiece of Western classical music and is one of the best-known symphonic works in music. It is the most frequently performed symphonic work in the world. The concert will include Olly Wilson’s Shango Memory, a modern piece that serves as a tribute to a Nigerian deity and the cultural contributions of the African diaspora. Vocal soloists include soprano Angel Blue, mezzo-soprano Tamara Mumford, tenor Ben Bliss and bass Dashon Burton. Performances on October 19 and 21 begin at 7:30 p.m., with a 2 p.m. matinee on Sunday, October 22. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2023-24/MTT-Beethoven9 or call the box office at (415) 864-6000.

articles.text: A first of its kind exhibit, reception provides celebration of artists (See additional photos on pages 16 & 17.) The. Piedmont Center for the Arts was abuzz with friendly voices during the Art Walk’s Artist Reception. On Friday, September 29, artists with work on display at the Art Walk were invited to spend an evening socializing with other artists and art fans while enjoying hors d’oeuvres and refreshments. “I think it is very friendly,” smiled Raffi Zaroukian. “People are very supportive here. Piedmont is a community where people really look out for each other. It’s an art gathering without the high-nose thing, but the quality is still there.” Zaroukian was also smiling because his painting, Cudillero Fishing Village, Spain, sold for $395 – two days before the actual Art Walk. Despite the feelings of familiarity and camaraderie, this was the first time the Art Walk has hosted an exhibit at the Center for the Arts. Larraine Seiden, a founder of the Piedmont Art Walk, says that when they Cudillero Fishing Village, Spain, by Raffi Zaroukian, digital hand painting, Giclee Print on Metal, 30” x 20” started, a reception like this just wasn’t possible. “I started the Art Walk with Jon in June 2020 and it had to be very dispersed [due to COVID],” said Seiden. “We worked with the Piedmont Police Department to make sure it was okay under the regulations at the time, but I think we always envisioned having an artist reception because the artists never got to meet each other.” she added. “It’s something that we always felt was lacking in the event.” In a final thought, Zaroukian added that he thinks it is important to socialize with other artists. “Otherwise we will be pigeonholed in our own world. We all have our own ideas, but it’s great to see other mediums, other thoughts, and other ways of doing things. It’s inspirational.” Regina O’Connor (left) speaks to artist Larraine Seiden at the artist reception at the Center for the Arts.
articles.title: Where art walks, artists talk

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony, led by Music Director Joseph Young, will open the 2023-24 Symphonic Series with American Kaleidoscope on Sunday, October 15 at 4 p.m. at Zellerbach Hall. The first of four Symphonic Series performances, American Kaleidoscope will showcase the Marcus Roberts Trio’s virtuosic style in a jazz-infused performance of James P. Johnson’s Yamekraw: A Negro Rhapsody, in addition to George Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue. Audiences will also experience the rare harmonies of Samuel Barber’s Essay for Orchestra No. 2 and Peter S. Shin’s introspective score Relapse. “We open this season with a celebration of the American sound, showcasing the intersection of different musical styles and the richness of our country’s culture,” said Music Director Joseph Young, “Samuel Barber’s powerful second essay is unapologetic and a tour-de-force piece that highlights the neoclassical American style, while Berkeley’s own Peter S. Shin brings a new contemporary work to our stage. I’m excited to welcome the Marcus Roberts Trio as we pair the music of two important American composers: George Gershwin, whose work is widely recognized, and James P. Johnson, a composer hardly heard in orchestral music. This program is an exciting way for Berkeley Symphony to begin its season, inviting audiences to gain a deeper understanding of American orchestral jazz.” The Marcus Roberts Trio is a long-term musical partnership between pianist Marcus Roberts, the phenomenal drummer Jason Marsalis, and gifted bassist Rodney Jordan. articles.text: James Franco as Aaron Ralston in 127 Hours 127 Hours opens on an early April morning, 2003, well before sunlight. Aaron Ralston (James Franco), a 27-year-old engineer, packs light gear in a daypack intending to spend the day in the Blue John Canyon area, exploring some of Utah’s most breathtaking country. He drives to a trailhead, of sorts, and heads off on his mountain bike, pushing hard, exhilarated by the day and the breadth of the scenery and the cerulean sky overhead. Leaving the bike chained to a tree, he continues on foot, wearing only his pack containing a bottle of water, a little food, climbing rope, straps and carabiners. He meets two young women, Kristi (Kate Mara) and Megan (Amber Tamblyn). They spend time swimming in a stunningly beautiful, aqua blue underground pool before Aaron continues, again alone. He is experienced, familiar with the terrain, and fearless as he runs and jumps across open crevices and down cinnamon colored arroyos. While traversing a benignlooking crevice, he loses his footing and slides down a sheer wall with a sizable boulder behind him. He lands hard, as does the rock, which wedges his right arm tight against the side of the crevice. In a heartbeat, his circumstances change. What was a carefree, insouciant day is suddenly transformed into an existential crisis. He’s in real trouble. What happens next is chronicled in Ralston’s book, “The Rock and the Hard Place,” telling about his 127-hour ordeal, trapped with no good way to free himself. His only possible return to freedom is a passable multipurpose utility tool, his climbing gear, and one bottle of water. He had left the oranges and Gatorade in his car. It is an improbable story in a container movie in which a person is trapped in a confined space (an airplane, a deep cave, a panic room, etc.) and must find a way to survive. Hours pass and soon Ralston will run out of water and food and he will die, while hallucinating about family and his girlfriend, Rana (Clemence Poesy). He knows that he has cavalierly taken the day trip without telling anyone where he is going. His supplies are meager. No cell phone, no emergency equipment. He is completely alone and without hope. Danny Boyle (Trainspotting, Slumdog Millionaire, 28 Days), working with two cinematographers, Enrique Chediak and Anthony Dod Mantle, manages to create a compelling film, one that is intense and in its own way grimly surprising. As well, James Franco delivers a wonderful portrayal of Ralston as he struggles, courageously, to survive. The movie is gripping from first to last. 127 Hours. Directed by Danny Boyle. Starring James Franco, Amber Tamblyn, Kate Mara and Clemence Poesy. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated R. Released in 2011, Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Grab the youngsters and sit them down to see African Cats, a Disneynature production. The story, narrated by Samuel L. Jackson, is nicely told, and since this is Disney, the stars of the film are anthropomorphized, with names such as Sita, Layla, Fang and Mara. All are endowed with human characteristics, to include thought. In one scene a cub lion, Mara, looks at her father, Fang, and thinks, “He’s the best dad in the world.” But then Disney has been humanizing animals in animation, as well as documentaries, for decades. They know how to capture children’s attention while exposing them to greater themes. Set on an immense savanna in East Africa, the tale follows two families: a pride of lions and a single mother cheetah and her cubs. The lions are also raising cubs, a task that Fang, the alpha male, takes no part in. Just as he doesn’t hunt; he only shows up to dine, say, on the zebra du jour. What makes African Cats compelling, especially for young audiences, is the remarkable work of cinematographers Owen Newman and Sophie Darlington. Filmed in high definition, many of the tight shots – a lion’s paw, a mother licking and nurturing her cub, a male lion confronting an alligator – inherently pose the question: how was it done, so close and intimate? It’s astonishing footage. As well, the aerial shots of massive herds of wildebeests migrating across the savanna are breathtaking, these ungainly animals plunging up draws and across the river, driven by an instinct that is incomprehensible. There is also one scene when the clouds turn dark and cold, lightening splits the sky, and slanting rain falls. Sita and her cubs sit waiting, shivering from the wet, as do all of the animals of the savanna. This moment is contrasted with the magnificent sunrises and sunsets that fill the horizons of these plains. Yet all is framed by the reality that the animals of the savanna face a harsh existence, focused daily on survival. At no time does the documentary’s voice over become pedantic, drifting into explanations about the shrinking habitat of these animals. If the migration route of the wildebeest is altered or truncated, for example, the ripple effect for other animals, such as the big cats of Africa, is significant. For now, however, as the credits roll, all is good. African Cats. Disneynature documentary. Directed by Alastair Fothergill and Keith Scholey. Photographed by Owen Newman and Sophie Darlington. 1 hr., 20 min. Rated G. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Disney+/Apple tv. T TH HE E

As well, the aerial shots of massive herds of wildebeests migrating across the savanna are breathtaking, these ungainly animals plunging up draws and across the river, driven by an instinct that is incomprehensible. There is also one scene when the clouds turn dark and cold, lightening splits the sky, and slanting rain falls. Sita and her cubs sit waiting, shivering from the wet, as do all of the animals of the savanna. This moment is contrasted with the magnificent sunrises and sunsets that fill the horizons of these plains. Yet all is framed by the reality that the animals of the savanna face a harsh existence, focused daily on survival. At no time does the documentary’s voice over become pedantic, drifting into explanations about the shrinking habitat of these animals. If the migration route of the wildebeest is altered or truncated, for example, the ripple effect for other animals, such as the big cats of Africa, is significant. For now, however, as the credits roll, all is good. African Cats. Disneynature documentary. Directed by Alastair Fothergill and Keith Scholey. articles.text: Alexander Valley is an area north of Napa Valley that that is not as well known as Napa but that also has an ideal climate for growing grapes and making wine. Soda Rock Winery is an historic property built in 1869 that was once the site of the Alexander Valley general store and post office and was the central hub of activity for the valley. The first winery on the site was bonded in 1880 and operated for many years before being abandoned. In 2000 Ken and Diane Wilson of Wilson Family Wines purchased the property and set about the arduous task of restoring the landmark property which had fallen into serious disrepair. The restoration was eventually completed and the winery was brought back to life. The location also serves as a popular event space for weddings and other social gatherings as the site regains its place as the hub of activity for the valley. In 2019 disaster struck and the Kincaid fire burned the winery to the ground. Once again, the Wilsons have set about restoring the property, with work still underway. Miraculously an old wooden structure next to the winery called “The Barn” survived the fire and now serves as the tasting room for Soda Rock Wines. They also have a tasting room in downtown Healdsburg. I recently had the opportunity to visit The Barn for a comprehensive tasting of the Soda Rock wines. I was hosted by the garrulous Jim Ferguson from Wilson Wines who has spent a lifetime in the wine industry and has an astoundingly comprehensive knowledge of California wines. Like the other Wilson wineries, I have visited and written about – Mazzoco, Pezzi King, Jaxon Keys, and Wilson – the wines from Soda Rock were uniformly well made and had a great quality/price ratio. The winemaker is the talented Antoine Favero who also makes wines at Mazocco and Jaxon Keys. Listed below are gems of Alexander Valley, with some amusing names. All are well worth searching out. If you’re a fan of soft cookies, try these for this pumpkin-spice season. This recipe comes together quickly. You mix everything by hand in just a few minutes and likely have most of the ingredients in your pantry. (If you don’t stock up on canned pumpkin, I highly recommend having a few on hand as they are hard to find in the off season.) I am partial to letting cookie dough rest in the ‘fridge overnight before baking. The flour has time to absorb the moist ingredients. In this case the overnight rest gives time for the spices to develop fuller flavor. It also firms up the dough, making for easier scooping. Note: This recipe uses one cup of canned pumpkin, leaving a bit more than one-half cup from the can. Do not discard it. I transfer it to a glass container and store it covered in the fridge for another use. Examples are adding it to a marinara sauce, vegetable soup broth, or even using it for pumpkin pancakes or waffles. • • pumpkin pie mix 1 teaspoon vanilla extract 1 extra-large egg, room temperature 1 cup bittersweet chocolate chips INSTRUCTIONS Pumpkin Chocolate Chip Cookies Adapted from Food52, Merrill Stubbs Makes 40 cookies, about 2” round INGREDIENTS • • • • • • • • • • • • 2 cups all-purpose flour 1 teaspoon ground cinnamon 1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg 1/2 teaspoon ground ginger 1/8 – 1/4 teaspoon ground cloves 1/2 teaspoon sea salt 2 teaspoons baking powder 1 teaspoon baking soda 1/2 cup light brown sugar, gently packed 1/2 cup granulated sugar 1/2 cup vegetable oil, neutral flavor 1 cup canned pumpkin, NOT In a medium bowl, whisk together the dry ingredients and set aside. In a large mixing bowl, whisk together the sugars, oil, pumpkin, vanilla, and egg until smooth. Add the dry ingredients to the wet and stir until just combined. Add the chocolate chips. Do not overmix. Cover tightly, then refrigerate the dough for several hours until chilled thoroughly, up to overnight is fine. When ready to bake, position two racks at the lower and upper thirds levels in the oven. Preheat to 350°F. Line two baking sheets with parchment paper. Scoop by tablespoonfuls onto parchment paper leaving about one inch between the cookies. Bake for about 12 - 14 minutes. Rotate the cookie sheets front to back and rack to rack if needed for even baking. Test for doneness by inserting a toothpick into the center of a cookie. It should come out clean. Cool on a wire rack for a few minutes. Remove the cookies with a thin spatula and finish cooling directly on a wire rack. Remember: they are delicate so take care when handling. These will keep in an air-tight container for several days. Separate any layering of cookies with a sheet of waxed paper to prevent sticking. They also freeze well. Place a single layer of baked cookies on a waxed paper lined sheet and freeze until firm. Transfer them into an airtight container for longer storage, up to about one month. A living trust can hold a person’s financial assets and other property while the trustee manages the money and makes investment and spending decisions. A living trust can be complex, so before establishing one, you’ll need to consult with your legal and tax professionals. articles.text: Hugh Smith, a lifelong Piedmont resident, passed away in the early hours of August 16, 2023 after a year-long battle with a heart condition. Born Hugh Langmuir Smith on December 10, 1953 in Oakland, he was raised by his parents in Piedmont. Growing up he became very involved in the Boy Scouts and earned the honor of Eagle Scout with Troop 11. One of Hugh’s more memorable experiences was traveling to Japan for the World Jamboree in 1971, where he weathered out a typhoon in a tent with his troopmates. It was in high school when he and his wife Victoria met and dated for the first time. After graduating from high school, Hugh took a three-month backpacking trip with friends through Europe, which sparked his lifelong love of travel. He went on to earn his Bachelor of Science in Business Administration from Cal State Hayward. Hugh’s business savvy led him into management at multiple Bay Area stores, as well as his own entrepreneurial ventures like the Left Hand Supply Company and a travel agency. He and his wife Victoria owned and operated AVB Travel for 25 years. Hugh came to specialize in cruises, and was affectionately known as the ‘Cruise Dude’ by many. He was proud to have visited all seven continents, stepping foot on the final one, Australia at the start of 2020. Hugh was married to his beloved Victoria for 40 years. In that time, the two returned to Piedmont, raised their two daughters, traveled the world, and often got the family together for holidays and barbecues. He was a kind and supportive father. He was excited to be part of field trips and homework help, made sure to teach his daughHugh Smith, born and raised in Piedmont, passed away on August 16. Hugh was skilled in home projects, garden care, and never missed a chance for spontaneous adventures. People often came to him for his encyclopedic knowledge of all things, from cars to history. He was a voracious reader and loved to learn about the world around him. To his friends and family, Hugh was known for his humor and relentless puns, warm and welcoming personality, and curiosity. He will be greatly missed by those who loved him. He is predeceased by longtime Piedmont residents, parents Daniel and Mary Smith, and brother Howard Smith. articles.text: Pamela Wells Rafanelli, a resident of Piedmont for nearly 50 years, passed away peacefully on August 27 in Carnelian Bay, California. Born Pamela Wells on July 24, 1946 in Oakland, she was the daughter of Walter M. Wells, Jr. and Mary Louise Wells. She spent her youth in Corte Madera and Santa Rosa. She and her brother, Steve Wells, were very close and treasured their family camping and fishing adventures. Pam graduated from the University of California, Berkeley with a degree in History and French. Her passion for learning history and languages through books, museums, and travel continued her entire life. She began her life-long teaching career in Cupertino before moving to Piedmont in 1973. During the early years of teaching, she earned a Master’s degree in education, specializing in early childhood learning differences. She was a beloved teacher to generations of students who attended Havens or Beach School during the 39 years in which she taught in Piedmont School District, with a particular love for teaching second grade. In addition to being a dedicated teacher, Pam raised four daughters, participated in multiple book clubs, hiked and cycled across California, volunteered at the Oakland Museum of California, and traveled the world. This past May, Pam took Paris by storm as she participated in an art history trip, climbed to the top of the Arc de Triomphe, and walked miles each day to revisit some of her favorite museums and sites. One of Pam’s favorite places in the world was Lake Tahoe. Her lakeside home offered her a stunning view of the lake and mountains and allowed her to sip her morning mug of coffee from a kayak in the waters of Carnelian Bay. Pam was an incredible baker and cook. She made ravioli from scratch for family reunions, baked baguettes for family dinners, and created desserts for every get-together. She knew to bake twice as many holiday cookies as were needed, since half disappeared during the family decorating process. Pam’s greatest joy came from spending time with any (or all!) of her 13 grandchildren. articles.text: On a beautiful Fall day, a strong turnout of 50 walkers and two K-9 best friends showed up for the weekly Walking on Wednesdays on September 27. A recent article in the Post by Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi on Wallace Alexander provided an inspiration for the day’s walk. The walkers were asked what historical figures they could think of who have Piedmont streets or buildings named after them. Frank C. Havens, Walter Blair, Hugh Craig, and even Isaac Requa came to mind; but Wallace Alexander was not named. Though he made many significant contributions to Piedmont, there is no public recognition of him. Drawing on Gail’s article, titled “Wallace M. Alexander - Piedmont’s Philanthropist,” the group learned about Alexander and his contributions. In 1912 he was instrumental in the construction of Piedmont’s first commercial center, today’s location of Wells Fargo Bank. In 1916 he arranged for the purchase of land for the Piedmont Interdenominational Church, now the Piedmont Community Church. Next, he organized the purchase in 1921 of land from the widow of Frank C. Havens for the construction of Piedmont High School. Additionally, Alexander helped establish and support the Piedmont Boy Scout Council in 1921. The walkers wanted to see some of Alexander’s legacy. They went past the former Piedmont commercial center, then across Highland Way to the Piedmont Scout Council office and the Community Church. They went up Mountain Avenue, but when they got to Bellevue, they were shocked to see that the giant sequoia at the traffic circle at Mountain and Bellevue Avenues was no longer there. For several years the City had the tree on a health watch list. It had gotten worse and arborists recommended removal before it fell over. The walkers followed Sea View to the northern edge of Alexander’s former estate, which ran from 87 Sea View to Hampton Road. More of Alexander’s history was shared. He was born in Maui in 1869, where his family was a leader in the Hawaiian sugar industry. They moved to the Bay Area so that Wallace could attend school in Oakland. He married his Oakland High School classmate, Mary Baker, in 1904, and they chose a large site on the corner of Sea View and Hampton, which was then called Union Street, for their home. The Alexanders built a threestory mansion that they named “Brown Gables” for its large, brown painted dormers. There was also a carriage house, which is now the home at 84 King Avenue. In 1911 Alexander’s mother built her own home at 92 Sea View across the street from Brown Gables, and his wife’s mother built a home further down the street at 236 Sea View. These homes are still there, but Brown Gables no longer exists. After Alexander died from a stroke in 1939, his wife followed his wish that the mansion be torn down, and the land subdivided into 13 lots so that more families could live in Piedmont. The walkers continued on to 92 Sea View, a 15,650-squarefoot home. An interesting reminder of the Alexanders is seen in inlays in the sidewalk that spell the word “Kailani.” the name of the Alexander family home in Hawaii. The walkers then crossed Hampton to see the home of Mary’s mother at 236 Sea View, which is now for sale. For $7,950,000 this 6,966-square-foot piece of history can be yours. The group then went on Farragut Avenue to King Avenue to see the Alexanders’ former carriage house at 84 King, currently being extensively remodeled. Across the street is Crocker Park, the land which Alexander donated to the City. The walkers continued up to Lincoln Avenue and back to the city center with a better understanding of Wallace Alexander’s service to Piedmont. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: On Friday, September 22, Piedmont bid farewell to a historic sequoia tree at the corner of Bellevue and Mountain Avenues. The City of Piedmont made the decision to remove the tree upon the recommendation of arborists hired by the city. Originally planted in 1890, the arborists determined that the tree had a significant lean and posed a safety risk for nearby homes. “It’s always painful to remove a prominent tree,” said Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works. “These trees have a history in the community.” The sequoia was the city’s official Christmas tree throughout the 1930s up until the beginning of World War II. Every year, the tree was decorated with lights and tinsel in anticipation of the holidays. The Public Works Department notified more than 80 of the homes closest to the tree to give residents time to say their goodbyes, but “there’s not a lot of time when arborists say they have to move on it quickly,” Gonzales said. “When the report came back this time, it said we should ‘look to remove it immediately.’ We don’t usually get that.” The sequoia has been in PiedStanding next to the sequoia tree in 1936 is Ah Foo who originally planted the tree. The sequoia tree had a significant lean which arborists determined was a risk to nearby homes. mont since 1890, making it 133 years old at the time of removal. The tree was planted by Ah Foo, an immigrant from China, who worked for a family on Bellevue and thought his employers’ orchard could use some beautification. The sapling he placed in that orchard grew into a large, healthy sequoia. When it came time to subdivide what was then the Bellevue district, the City thought that Foo’s tree was too beautiful to cut down. So, the City built around it and the tree settled into the position it would take for the next 100 years. Cameron Wolfe with the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) shared Gonzales’ somber assessment of the situation but admits that the tree’s removal was inevitable. “It was only a matter of time before it was going to have to come down,” said Wolfe. “Thank goodness they got it before any damage was done. You could see from the way it was leaning that it could have fallen and done immense damage to some beautiful pieces of property.” Wolfe went on to say that sequoia gigantea — as the tree is scientifically known — more typically grow at elevations of 5,000 feet or higher as opposed to Piedmont’s 300 feet. The tree’s unique position in the middle of a rotunda at a street intersection meant very little water could get to it. In other words, the sequoia wasn’t thriving where it was planted. “The good news is that we got every ounce of enjoyment that tree could give us. It was such a long-living tree in such dire circumstances… So, it was a valiant tree, let’s put it that way,” explained Wolfe. “It’s going to be fun to see what comes in its place. I’m sure it will not be a sequoia because that would be inviting a repeat of a sad story. And I’m sure it won’t be a Cypress, but I think there’ll be a consensus and I’m actually excited to see what happens to that location.” A contractor begins removal of the historic sequoia tree at Bellevue & Mountain Avenues. After removal, the stump of the once-towering sequoia gigantea sits within its’ traffic circle.

You could see from the way it was leaning that it could have fallen and done immense damage to some beautiful pieces of property.” Wolfe went on to say that sequoia gigantea — as the tree is scientifically known — more typically grow at elevations of 5,000 feet or higher as opposed to Piedmont’s 300 feet. The tree’s unique position in the middle of a rotunda at a street intersection meant very little water could get to it. In other words, the sequoia wasn’t thriving where it was planted. “The good news is that we got every ounce of enjoyment that tree could give us. It was such a long-living tree in such dire circumstances… So, it was a valiant tree, let’s put it that way,” explained Wolfe. “It’s going to be fun to see what comes in its place. I’m sure it will not be a sequoia because that would be inviting a repeat of a sad story. And I’m sure it won’t be a Cypress, but I think there’ll be a consensus and I’m actually excited to see what happens to that location.” A contractor begins removal of the historic sequoia tree at Bellevue & Mountain Avenues. After removal, the stump of the once-towering sequoia gigantea sits within its’ traffic circle.

articles.text: Photo by Jeff Hansen Police blocked off part of Grand Avenue after two people were arrested for attempted car theft. “Hey, someone’s breaking into your car,” whispered a coworker to Adele Pease. Tuesday, October 3 at around 2 p.m. marked the second time this month someone had broken into her car. It was even on the same street as last time. When she arrived at her car, her window was smashed in and the wires under her steering wheel were ripped out. Someone had tried to hotwire her car. That’s when she saw two figures sprinting in opposite directions on Boulevard Way near the corner of Grand Avenue. “At that point, a man came up [to me] and said that he had called 911,” said Pease. “That’s when all the police started coming,” added an eyewitness who has asked to remain anonymous. “Undercover police cars came out of nowhere chasing someone into Piedmont,” the witness added. “You wouldn’t have even known they were undercover [police] until their lights started flashing.” The suspects allegedly hid between houses in the area after Staff photo Piedmont and Oakland police officers on Grand Avenue gather to take statements after an attempted car theft. their theft attempt before running away. Piedmont and Oakland police arrived within minutes and both suspects were apprehended. Both suspects were juveniles wearing black hooded sweatshirts with camouflage bandanas covering the lower half of their faces. “We’re just grateful to have a good relationship with Oakland PD,” said Piedmont Police Captain Chris Monahan. “One of our officers was at the right place at the right time, and with their assistance we were able to Staff photo An officer walks a detained suspect to the back of a police car. arrest the juvenile suspects in question. It’s all about collaboration and we’re grateful for the opportunity to collaborate with Oakland PD.” “The officer [I talked to] told me to buy a new car, and ‘maybe not invest in a KIA,’” said Pease. KIA model cars have been a frequent target of car thefts in recent months because of their lack of security measures. There are several methods that criminals can use to easily start the car without keys. There are also videos online detailing these methods step by step. The anonymous witness said that he doubted anything would happen to the two suspects because they were minors. “They’re being cooperative [with police officers], but they’re smiling like it’s nothing,” he said. Pease said that she believes that strong community ties are important for maintaining public safety in light of these events. “I think that making sure that you’re in contact with your neighbors and having a better community is what needs to happen. We just need to be watching each other’s back,” said Pease.
